title: useState & functional updates
objectives: Predict what repeated setState calls in one handler produce, given state is a per-render snapshot
Choose the functional updater form whenever the next state is computed from the previous state
Fix stacked updates that lose increments by rewriting setX(x + 1) as setX(prev => prev + 1)

sources.title: React docs: Queueing a Series of State Updates
React docs: State as a Snapshot

questions.prompt: count starts at 0. In one click handler you call setCount(count + 1) three times. What is count on the next render?

options.text: It throws — you can't call setState twice

questions.explanation: During a render, `count` is a fixed snapshot (0). All three calls compute 0 + 1 = 1, and React batches them, so the result is 1. Use the functional updater setCount(c => c + 1) — each call receives the latest value — to get 3.

questions.prompt: When should you use the functional updater form, setX(prev => ...)?

options.text: When the next value is computed from the previous value
Always — the direct form setX(value) is deprecated
Never — it's only for class components

questions.explanation: Reach for setX(prev => ...) whenever the new state depends on the old — multiple updates in one handler, updates inside async callbacks/closures, or anywhere the closed-over value might be stale. If you're setting a fresh value that doesn't read the old one, the direct form is fine.

prompts.prompt: Rewrite this increment so three calls in a row reliably add 3, not 1.
prompts.explanation: The functional updater setCount(c => c + 1) hands you React's most up-to-date value instead of the render-time snapshot, so stacked updates compound correctly. The parameter name is yours to choose (c, prev, n…).

snippets.question: After clicking the button once, what does it show?
snippets.explanation: Both calls read the same snapshot count = 0, so both set 1. React batches them into one re-render → 1, not 2.

snippets.question: After clicking once, what does it show now?
snippets.explanation: Each updater receives the result of the previous one: 0 → 1 → 2. Functional updates queue and compound, so you get 2.
